Jarren Duran's Platoon Pattern Against Lefties
Duran bats left-handed, Gore throws left-handed, and Boston's coaching staff has ceased to start Duran on days a southpaw takes the mound for the opponent.
Nate Eaton takes over in center field for Boston.
Texas had already turned in its own lineup behind Gore hours before first pitch, setting up the Wednesday matchup at Globe Life Field.
Duran's absence from the lineup against lefties has stretched to seven straight starts without facing a southpaw, dating back to his last look at left-handed pitching on Aug. 8, according to RotoWire. He sat again Sunday against Kansas City and was used only as a pinch-hitter, a role he has filled repeatedly this month.
There is no reported health issue behind Tracy's decision. Duran started Tuesday against right-hander Jacob deGrom, playing center field and batting seventh, and remains fully active on Boston's roster.
Duran is slashing .204/.261/.361 with 20 home runs across 141 games this season, and his OPS against left-handed pitching sits at .641, actually higher than his .616 mark against right-handers, according to FanGraphs. Boston has kept sitting him against lefties anyway.

Duran's Playing Time Has Dropped Sharply
Duran appeared in 160 games in 2024, when he led the American League in at-bats, doubles and triples, on his way to an All-Star selection and an eighth-place MVP finish. He followed that with 157 games in 2025.
This year he has played in 141 of Boston's games, a drop that traces to the growing run of benchings against left-handed hurlers. Wednesday marks at least the seventh time this season Boston has parked Duran for a left-handed starter, following earlier sit-downs against Rodón, Kyle Freeland, Jacob Lopez, Mitch Bratt and Reid Detmers, according to CBS Sports.
Boston opened the year with four outfielders competing for time, but an early injury to Roman Anthony briefly opened the picture before Duran struggled through a rough first half, batting .194 over his first 87 games. The Duran platoon has held even as the outfield picture has grown thinner. Ceddanne Rafaela remains out with a quad injury and Eli White is sidelined with a foot issue, leaving Eaton as the only regular right-handed option in center on days Duran sits.
With the Red Sox pushing for playoff position down the stretch, Duran's shrinking role against left-handed pitching will keep drawing scrutiny. Entering Wednesday's game, the Red Sox magic number for clinching a playoff berth is five — meaning that any combination of Red Sox wins and Chicago White Sox losses totaling five puts Boston in the postseason.

Since returning from injury on August 30, Roman Anthony has looked more like the 2025 version of himself than he did at the beginning of the season. He's hitting .258 with a .764 OPS. In his 15 games, he's got five RBI and six extra-base hits; it's good for a 109 WRC+. It's exactly what the Red Sox needed from him in his return from his May 4 injury.
The one thing Anthony has struggled with has been leading off the game. He has hit leadoff in every game he's played since his return and has only two singles, a double, and five strikeouts with no walks in that spot. It's probably time to have someone else lead off.
In his absence (May 5-August 29), Red Sox leadoff hitters had success in the first inning. While they only hit .213, they had a .307 on-base percentage and a .449 slugging percentage, which equated to a 108 WRC+. Surprisingly, most of that success came from Jarren Duran, who hit leadoff 31 of the 101 games and had a 141 WRC+.
Roman Anthony hasn't performed in the first inning, but he has the rest of the game
Anthony has struggled in the leadoff spot all season. In a total of 36 games, the lefty has a .299 OPS in the first inning. In the second inning or later this season, Anthony boasts a .280/.395/.439/.834 slash line and a 136 WRC+. In those same innings, in only the games he was first in the batting order, he has a .792 OPS and 125 WRC+.
Something about him batting first in the first inning isn't working for him. Whether it's his approach or the way pitchers are attacking him in that spot, Anthony hasn't been able to put it together this season. That's why it's time to drop him down in the order.
That doesn't mean to all of a sudden move him down to seventh in the order, but to push him down to second or third and put a player with high on-base skills in front of him. The Sox have had a few players show really great on-base skills this season. Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, and Isiah Kiner-Falefa are all players with an OBP over .340 this season. Having one of them leadoff, then getting on base in front of Anthony, Ceddanne Rafaela, Willson Contreras, and Wilyer Abreu would be extremely dangerous.
Anthony hasn't shown he can hack it leading off the game this season; it's been his one real weak point since his return. With two weeks until the start of the playoffs and a postseason berth almost assured (100% per FanGraphs as of September 15th), now is the time to experiment with the lineup and fix this problem before they get to October.

The Boston Red Sox are in the middle of a postseason push this September, but one the 2026 season comes to a close, there are going to be some huge questions the Red Sox will need to answer.
Whether it's about the future of Jarren Duran in the outfield, or how the team will handle the infield setup with Franklin Arias potentially an option, this is a very important offseason. But one of the keys to the offseason will revolve around Sonny Gray.
Tim Kelly of Bleacher Report highlighted the $30 million question the Red Sox will have with Gray this fall and winter. With a $30M mutual option, the Red Sox are at real risk of losing Gray to the open market this offseason.
Red Sox facing tricky $30M Sonny Gray problem
"Considering he'll pitch next season at 37, he's probably not going to get more than $30 million for 2027 as a free agent," Kelly writes. "However, if he declines the option, the Red Sox will owe him a $10 million buyout."
Boston is surely going to accept their side of the $30 million mutual option, considering how great Gray has been for the Red Sox this season.
But when it comes to whether Gray will accept the option or not, this $10 million buyout presents a big problem for the Red Sox.
It would not be a surprise if Gray declined the option, got the $10M buyout from the Red Sox, and then sought out a $20 million per-year contract.
Even though Gray is older, some team, whether it's the Red Sox or another club, will surely be willing to spend $20 million to land Gray.
But what makes it so tricky is that Gray could sign a two-year, $40 million deal on the open market, guaranteeing he lands an extra $20 million in 2028, regardless of his performance and health during the 2027 season.
He has a 2.76 ERA and a 17-5 record with the Red Sox in 2026, and is deserving of a big contract if he hits the open market. Even though he's older, his incredible 2026 season could present a challenge for the Red Sox.
Teams are going to have interest in Gray, and his $30 million option presents a big problem for the Red Sox. They could be out a key starter and lose some money in the process. This is a tricky situation, and one Craig Breslow needs to manage well.

Red Sox Video
The Boston Red Sox are a near-lock for the second AL Wild Card spot. With just over 10 games left in the season, it’d take a whole mess of crazy for the Sox to move up or down. While it would be great to have a shot at moving up in the standings, their current situation will allow them to spend the final two weeks of the season freshening up their stalwarts, getting injury returnees back up to speed, and fixing Jarren Duran.
Duran hasn’t quite been the worst regular in Major League Baseball, but that’s damning with faint praise. He’s still an excellent baserunner and a plus fielder, but only Ezequiel Tovar has a lower wRC+ (51) among qualified hitters than Duran’s mark of 67. Despite his disintegrated noodle of a bat, he has racked up 578 plate appearances due to injuries and, presumably, a lack of better options, but that doesn’t make him a lost cause.
What makes Duran’s complete collapse at the plate so shocking is that he was a top-25 hitter by wRC+ only two seasons ago (132), and well above average just last season (112). While it’s safe to assume 2024 was a career year, he looked to have established himself as an above-average bat, and it’s not like all of his underlying metrics have cratered. If anything, many have improved.
He’s swinging the bat as fast as ever. His barrel rate is almost identical to the past two seasons. He’s pulling the ball in the air more. And while his in-zone contact rate is a career-low 84%, that’s a completely fair trade-off for what should be better power.
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
| | | | | |
Now, you could argue that Duran didn’t need to change his approach from 2024, but given these figures, there’d be no reason to believe he had gone from one of the best hitters in baseball to almost the very worst. However, this chart doesn’t contain every last kernel of underlying data, and the one thing that has cratered for Duran is the most basic, fundamental skill of hitting—not chasing (f***ing) fastballs out of the zone.
Duran is running a wRC+ of 67 because his out-of-zone swing rate (O-Swing%) has ballooned to 34.5%, which is largely driven by a career-high O-Swing% of 36.8% against four-seam fastballs. Throughout his career, Duran’s production has largely followed his ability to lay off pitches out of the zone, but his inability to lay off four-seam fastballs (FA), to this degree, is new.
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
| | | | |
What makes his cratering performance against four-seamers so baffling is that it is exclusively down to swing decisions. His production when he makes contact is relatively unchanged, and he’s not whiffing a concerning amount in the zone. In fact, his zone contact rate against four-seamers is better than it was in 2024.
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
| | | | | | | |
It’s not groundbreaking analysis to say that swinging at fastballs out of the zone is a bad idea, but it doesn’t necessarily doom a hitter to the abyss. However, Duran’s ability against four-seamers was a load-bearing trait, and it becoming a weakness has completely collapsed his profile because it has cost him the platoon advantage.
Unsurprisingly, Duran, a left-handed hitter, has made a career out of pulverizing right-handed pitching. His career wRC+ against righties is 114, compared to 72 against lefties. Splits like this are far from unusual, but what has happened to Duran in 2026 is. Over 410 plate appearances against righties, he has a wRC+ of 63. That’s the second-worst among qualified hitters, and it all stems from his struggles against four-seam fastballs.
This season, 37.3% of the pitches right-handers have thrown Duran have been four-seam fastballs, right in line with his career average of 38.7%. While four-seamers generally have more neutral platoon splits, historically, Duran absolutely feasted on right-handed four-seamers. Entering 2026, Duran had a +20.6 run value against right-handed four-seam fastballs, but he has somehow managed an absolutely preposterous, incomprehensible -13.1 run value in 2026.
The reason why Duran’s plate discipline has completely collapsed against four-seamers is a bit more of a mystery, but I think it starts with his increased desire to swing hard, lift, and pull. Over the past four seasons, as Duran’s swing speed has increased, he has hit the ball out in front a bit more.
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
| | | |
None of this is particularly surprising and should be expected. A faster bat will make contact out in front more often, and bat speed increases throughout a swing. The two moving in tandem make all the sense in the world, but getting to this point could have come at a cost.
To sell out for swing speed and contact out in front, Duran likely has to get his operation started just a fraction of a second earlier, which means committing to pitches a tad earlier as well. The trickle-down effect is swinging at more pitches out of the zone, and in particular four-seam fastballs, which require the quickest decisions at the plate.
The Red Sox don’t need Jarren Duran to figure it out to make the playoffs, but getting him back to basics could unlock another level of the offense. With Duran producing at an average offensive level, suddenly the Sox could field an elite outfield defense of Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, and Duran, while letting Roman Anthony DH. However, for that dream arrangement to work, Duran needs to actually hit again, and that starts with laying off fastballs outside of the zone.

ARLINGTON, Texas — The Red Sox didn’t have many big swings Tuesday night against Jacob deGrom and the Rangers, but one from a late-game pinch-hitter nearly flipped the script on the whole night.
Pinch-hitting for Jarren Duran against All-Star closer Jacob Latz in the eighth inning with Boston trailing by two, Andruw Monasterio got a 3-2 fastball just below the zone and smoked it — just foul. Monasterio sent a screaming line drive down the left field line, but it landed in the seats in foul territory, 369 feet away from home plate. If the ball had landed a few feet to its right, the Red Sox would have led 6-4 heading into the ninth.
For a second, the Red Sox dugout (on the third base side) thought Monasterio was a hero.
“It’s hard to tell from the dugout, from our angle,” said interim manager Chad Tracy. “When it came off the bat, it looked like, ‘Is that gonna hit the foul pole?’ But for about halfway on the ball flight, it was like, ‘I think that might hit the foul pole, I think it might be close.’”
Instead, Monasterio’s at-bat continued and Latz blew a 97 mph fastball by him to escape the threat. It was the second bases-loaded escape for the Rangers, who also didn’t allow a run in a similar situation in the fifth. In all, the Red Sox were hitless in four at-bats with runners in scoring position and left nine on base.
“We gave ourselves a couple of opportunities to maybe hit a single and tie the game up,” Tracy said. “We just couldn’t do it tonight.”
The pressure-filled situation marked just Monasterio’s 12th plate appearance in 15 games since Trevor Story and Roman Anthony were both activated from the injured list August 30.
Sandoval struggles
When starter Patrick Sandoval struck out the first four batters of his outing, it looked like he was about to go toe-to-toe with deGrom, the five-time All-Star on the other side. But that illusion quickly collapsed in a brutal second inning in which Sandoval allowed four runs and threw 44 pitches.
Sandoval allowed two separate rallies as the Rangers scored four times with two outs. With two men on after both singled, Elias Díaz opened the scoring with a two-run double to left. Sandoval then walked two batters in a row before Corey Seager plated two runs with a bloop single to left-center.
“Just got to pitch better,” said Sandoval, who has a 4.99 ERA. “Got to do better for this team. Can’t be doing this.”
Sandoval was the victim of some bad luck as Seager’s single left the bat at just 67.2 mph and traveled 212 feet. The ball fell in no man’s land between Story and Anthony and glanced off Story’s glove. Still, Sandoval took the blame.
“Just got to make a better pitch,” Sandoval said. “That’s it.”
Sandoval lasted just 2 ⅔ innings in Boston’s 4-2 loss, allowing four earned runs on four hits while walking two batters. He did have five strikeouts.
Sogard homers again
The only scoring of the night for the Red Sox came in the third when Nick Sogard launched a line-drive two-run shot off deGrom that tucked inside the right field foul pole. Considering Boston had just three hits against deGrom, it was an impressive swing on a slider down and in.
“I’d only gotten one fastball that at-bat and it was kinda up-and-in, so with two strikes, he likes to back-foot it,” Sogard said. “One of the best pitchers in the game. Ton of respect for him. But I had a feeling it was going to be something in. I definitely wasn’t sitting on it. I was a little out in front, but I was able to keep it fair and it got over the wall.”
Sogard waited a while for his first big league homer, going 321 plate appearances before going deep against Arizona on August 19. Including Tuesday, he has now homered five times in his last 99 trips to the plate.
“I feel good,” he said. “Just trying to compete and grind out good at-bats and get your pitches to hit. I’ve been able to drive it a little bit better this year.”
Bullpen strategy keeps options open
When Tracy pulled Sandoval with two outs in the third and Wyatt Langford coming to the plate, he went to righty Brayan Bello, a common piggyback option who has given the Red Sox plenty of long relief appearances and threw 103 pitches in his last outing, a start against the Angels on Labor Day. But Tracy chose to only use Bello for 1 ⅔ innings (and 19 pitches). It was his shortest appearance of the year.
The reason, Tracy said, was to keep the possibility open for Bello to make a longer appearance (potentially a start) later in the week. Boston’s well-rested bullpen cobbled together the rest of the game with Bello (five outs), Alec Gamboa (three), Wyatt Olds (two) and Jovani Morán (six) passing the baton.
“We’re keeping options open,” said Tracy. “Part of the reason we were able to be so aggressive is that so much of the bullpen was at five, six or seven days off. Being able to spread the load a little bit and not overextend anybody, but also keeping options open if there is a start or something. We want to keep that on the table.
“We were able to do that today and piece it together with four guys instead of just having one guy take on the whole load.”

Patrick Sandoval has had a rocky month. Entering Tuesday, the Red Sox left-hander had allowed a 6.12 ERA over his last five starts, but coming out of the gate Sandoval looked like he’d finally figured things out.
But after striking out the first four batters he faced, the wheels came off in the bottom of the second.
Sandoval allowed four runs over an interminable 44-pitch second inning and ultimately got the hook after recording just eight outs in Boston’s 4-2 loss to the Texas Rangers.
Nick Sogard hit a two-run home run to help get the Red Sox back into the game, but the offense otherwise couldn’t get anything going against Jacob deGrom and the Rangers bullpen, squandering bases loaded opportunities in the fifth and eighth innings.
Sandoval started strong by striking out the side in the first inning, but after sending down Jake Burger to start the second everything ground to a screeching halt. The right-hander allowed a pair of singles, served up a two-run double to Elias Diaz, and then walked back-to-back batters to load the bases for five-time All-Star Corey Seager.
It appeared for a moment like Sandoval might minimize the damage when he drew a pop fly to shallow left, but the ball drifted into no-man’s land and Trevor Story couldn’t make the catch, allowing two more runs to score and putting the Rangers up 4-0.
Sandoval ultimately needed 44 pitches to get through the second, blowing up his pitch count and ensuring a long evening for the Red Sox bullpen. He recorded two outs in the third and was lifted for Brayan Bello after allowing four runs over 2 2/3 innings.
“They drug at bats out on him,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in Arlington postgame. “It looked like he was going to get out of there with Diaz, that was a long at bat, I think one of those pitches was close and then he hits the double in the corner and it was just a struggle, we just couldn’t get out of the inning.”
Four runs matches the largest deficit the Red Sox have overcome in a win this season, but the club didn’t need long to cut it in half. After Caleb Durbin reached on a one-out single in the top of the third, Sogard ripped a line drive off deGrom that cleared the right field fence for a two-run home run.
It was the fifth home run of the season for Sogard, all of which have come since Aug. 19. Prior to that the 29-year-old had never hit a homer over his first three seasons as a big leaguer.
That wound up being as close as Boston got.
The Red Sox could have tied the score or taken the lead with one swing in the fifth inning, but despite loading the bases without recording a hit the club couldn’t get a run across. Jarren Duran was hit by a pitch, Durbin reached on catcher’s interference and Mickey Gasper walked to bring up Adley Rutschman with two outs, but the catcher grounded out to short to keep it a 4-2 game.
Boston’s bullpen did its part to keep the Red Sox in the game. Bello tossed 1 2/3 perfect innings, Alec Gamboa threw one scoreless aided in large part by a brilliant double play turned by Sogard to end the fifth, and Wyatt Olds worked his way out of a runners-at-the-corners, two-out jam to escape the sixth. Jovani Moran entered with a man on in the seventh and got three quick outs, setting the table for one last Red Sox push in the eighth.
Jahmai Jones sparked the rally with a leadoff single, Willson Contreras drew a one-out walk, and after Wilyer Abreu grounded out to move the two runners into scoring position Story was intentionally walked to load the bases again.
Rather than have Duran face the left-hander Jacob Latz, Tracy pinch hit Andruw Monasterio, but the move didn’t pay off. Monasterio worked a full count and nearly went deep on a hard hit liner that landed just foul before striking out to leave them loaded again.
Boston went quietly in the top of the ninth, finishing the game 0 for 4 with runners in scoring position while stranding nine men on base.
“We gave ourselves a couple of opportunities to maybe hit a single and tie the game up and we couldn’t do it tonight,” Tracy said.
Magic number still 5
In addition to keeping pace in the AL West race, the Rangers also jumped the Toronto Blue Jays to become the first team below the AL Wild Card cutline. As a result the Red Sox’s magic number remains five despite the Blue Jays’ 10-1 loss earlier in the night.
Boston (82-69) can clinch a playoff berth as early as Friday, and depending on how things play out in the AL Central the Red Sox could lock down the second Wild Card spot as soon as this weekend.
Houck scoreless with WooSox
Tanner Houck (Tommy John surgery rehab) tossed a scoreless inning of relief in his latest rehab appearance with the WooSox on Tuesday. The right-hander entered the game in the seventh inning and allowed one walk, no hits and struck out three over 22 pitches.

The Boston Red Sox never fully resolved their outfield-designated hitter logjam, and once again it may create a roster conundrum. For much of the season, things had worked themselves out one way or another.
Spending most of the season without Roman Anthony certainly wasn't ideal, but it did make for a cleaner lineup card. His return, of course, has been music to our ears, and it saved the Red Sox from another tough roster decision due to the injuries to Masataka Yoshida and Ceddanne Rafaela.
There's a point where push might come to shove, though, and Boston is forced to make a tough choice. Chad Tracy won't rule out Yoshida returning in time for the playoffs, which would lead to some interesting decisions.
"He's [Yoshida] not on the 60-day (injured list). It's just a matter of how does he heal over the next handful of weeks," the interim skipper said.
If the 33-year-old can return in time for October, it could put the likes of Mickey Gasper or Nick Sogard in the crosshairs. At which point, the Red Sox will have to make a choice and leave someone unhappy.
Masataka Yoshida shouldn't cost Mickey Gasper or Nick Sogard a spot on the Red Sox playoff roster
Just because Yoshida can come back (and that's still up in the air) doesn't mean he should. The NPB veteran has done what he's always done since coming stateside, hit for some average and get on base, but has provided very little in the power department.
Through 87 games, he's hit .274/.347/.399 with five homers, which is nothing to sneeze at, but doesn't really scratch the Red Sox's power itch. On top of that, despite what we saw in the World Baseball Classic, he has little defensive value and will be a nonfactor in the outfield coming off a serious hamstring strain.
Comparatively, Gasper's hot bat better fits what Boston needs. While he might simply be riding the wave rather than emerging as a true offensive force, the switch-hitter has brought the pop with eight dingers in just 187 plate appearances and a .500 slugging percentage, all while providing similar contact and on-base numbers to Yoshida.
Furthermore, he has some value in the field with the ability to fill in behind the plate if needed, as well as play first base. That alone gives him an edge over the DH-only Yoshida.
As for Sogard, his offensive profile is similar to Yoshida's, but his positional versatility is far superior. Depending on Curtis Mead's recovery, Sogard is a valuable insurance policy at second base that should have him over Yoshida in the October pecking order, too.
Craig Breslow's failure to move Jarren Duran before he became a radioactive asset is the real key here. Not only does it represent a missed opportunity for the Red Sox, but it is also the main barrier for Yoshida, given that Boston can't really afford to carry a DH-only player. With that, the choice should be clear. Even if Yoshida is healthy, he needs to sit this October out.

We've reached the "wake me up for the playoffs" portion of the Boston Red Sox season.
The Red Sox have 12 games remaining on their 2026 regular-season schedule. As of Monday, they sit comfortably in the second American League Wild Card spot with a six-game lead. They're 4.5 games behind the New York Yankees in the Wild Card standings, so barring a shocking development, they'll visit the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series for the second consecutive year.
Which 26 players will the Red Sox bring with them to the Bronx? Who's on the chopping block? Here's our 26-man playoff roster projection with 15 days until Game 1:
MORE RED SOX
Catcher (2): Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
Cuts: None
The Red Sox could theoretically cut Wong since he'd barely see the field with Rutschman healthy. If Rutschman went down in that scenario, Mickey Gasper could go behind the plate... but that wouldn't be pretty.
Here's the problem with that approach: If Rutschman gets hurt and the Red Sox add a replacement catcher mid-series, Rutschman would be ineligible for the next playoff round. So if he got hurt in the Wild Card Series, he'd be ineligible for the ALDS and eligible to return in the ALCS.
Putting Wong on the playoff roster ensures that if Rutschman goes down, they won't need to add a mid-series replacement with Wong and Gasper already on board. And while Wong isn't exactly Pudge Rodriguez defensively, he's better than Gasper behind the dish.
Infield (7): Willson Contreras, Trevor Story, Caleb Durbin, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, Andruw Monasterio
Cuts: Curtis Mead (IL), Anthony Seigler (IL)
Even with Wong on the roster, Gasper's incredible offensive upside shown in August earns him a roster spot as a bench bat. Monasterio is on the bubble, but recent injuries may have cleared his path to a bench role.
It doesn't look like Mead (wrist) will be healthy in time for the start of the postseason.
Outfield (5): Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
Cuts: Eli White (IL), Masataka Yoshida (IL), Nate Eaton
The big question mark here is White's health, as the speedster was recently placed on the 10-day injured list with a foot ligament injury. He'll play a key bench role if healthy, but if he isn't, Jones or Eaton are the top candidates for that fifth outfield spot. We're leaning Jones because of his ability to mash left-handers.
Yoshida (hamstring) probably isn't coming back this year.
Starting rotation (3): Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suarez
Cuts: Patrick Sandoval
Sandoval just hasn't been reliable, so he draws the short straw. Jake Bennett and the returning Garrett Crochet move to the bullpen -- assuming Crochet is healthy enough to give one or two quality innings in relief.
Bullpen (9): Garrett Crochet, Jake Bennett, Brayan Bello, Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, Erik Miller, Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman
Cuts: Justin Slaten (IL), Tanner Houck (IL), Johan Oviedo (IL), Alec Gamboa, Jovani Moran, Raymond Burgos
If Slaten's elbow is healthy, he's in, but it doesn't currently look like it will be since he was recently shut down from throwing.
Crochet is trending toward being ready just in time for October. So is Houck, but he hasn't pitched in a big-league game since May 2025, and he hasn't looked sharp in his rehab outings. While his upside is intriguing, we'd leave him off the initial playoff roster.
Brayan Bello makes the cut as a bulk arm after excelling in that role throughout the second half.
